[INTERVIEW] Irene “DEE” Moore: Reclaiming Her Place In The BO$$ Legacy

  • November 17, 2026
  • Todd Davis
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 13:06
Instaread

Before Bo$$ became a force in Hip-Hop, there were two women from Detroit with something to prove, a dream bigger than their surroundings and absolutely no intention of waiting for permission. Lichelle Laws commanded the microphone. Irene “Dee” Moore commanded the turntables. Together, they set out to make their mark in a culture that wasn’t exactly rolling out the welcome mat for women who wanted more than a seat at the table.

Long before Born Gangstaz arrived in 1993, “Deeper” and “Recipe for a Hoe” helped define an era.

But Bo$$ began as a partnership between two young women with one shared vision. Their journey took them from Detroit to Los Angeles in pursuit of their dreams. They faced uncertainty, found their footing, and caught DJ Quik’s attention. That connection helped them secure a deal with Def Jam West and enter Hip-Hop history.

Advertisement

What followed was more than a breakthrough; it was a statement. Lichelle Laws entered a male-dominated arena with an unapologetic presence, commanding delivery, and a voice that demanded attention. As Bo$$, she helped create space for women in gangsta rap. She challenged expectations and left her mark with Born Gangstaz.

The album remains a defining piece of ’90s Hip-Hop. Lichelle’s contribution deserves recognition beyond records, charts, and headlines. She was a trailblazer who made her presence felt on her own terms. Her passing in March 2024 left a void, but her music continues to live on. Her legacy remains firmly rooted in Hip-Hop history.

But history has a way of remembering the name on the marquee while overlooking the people who helped build the stage. As Bo$$ transitioned from a duo into the solo recording identity of Lichelle Laws, Dee’s public visibility diminished, and much of her contribution to the group’s beginnings was left outside the larger narrative. That doesn’t erase her place in the story. It makes hearing her side of it all the more important. And recognizing Dee’s chapter doesn’t take anything away from Lichelle’s crown — it adds another dimension to the story of how Bo$$ came to be.

Advertisement

This story goes beyond nostalgia. It captures the music, the journey, the risks, the relationships, and the realities behind a groundbreaking moment in Hip-Hop. It also highlights the woman behind the decks and the creative partner who helped build Bo$$ before its breakthrough.

With Laws’ passing, preserving this history matters even more. The goal isn’t to rewrite anyone’s legacy, create controversy, or take away from Bo$$’s achievements. Instead, we want to celebrate Lichelle, honor their shared journey, and ensure future generations hear the complete story.

More than 30 years later, Irene “Dee” Moore steps back into the conversation to revisit the beginnings, the breakthrough, the music, the separation and the life beyond Bo$$. This is her perspective, her chapter and her opportunity to put her own words to a history she helped create — while paying tribute to the woman whose name became synonymous with a movement and whose music continues to speak.

Advertisement

The records still knock. The legacy still stands. Lichelle Laws made sure of that. And before the world knew Bo$$, there was Dee. It’s time to hear her — and remember the woman who helped make it all possible.

Parlé Mag: Growing up in Detroit, how did the city’s music and culture influence your love for Hip-Hop?
Irene “Dee” Moore: Growing up in Detroit, music was everywhere. Detroit has always been a city of soul, creativity, struggle, and determination. We had Motown, R&B, funk, and eventually hip-hop, and all those sounds influenced the culture around us. What attracted me to hip-hop was the freedom to express yourself. It was more than music; it was a movement. It gave people a voice, especially people whose stories weren’t always being heard. I wanted to be part of something real, something that represented our experiences. Detroit taught me to be strong, original, and never afraid to stand apart from the crowd.

Advertisement

Parlé Mag: How did you and Lichelle Laws first meet at Oakland University, and what brought you together creatively?
Irene “Dee” Moore: When Lichelle and I connected at Oakland University, music became something that brought us together. We shared an interest in hip-hop, but we also brought different creative qualities to the table. What made the partnership special was the possibility of combining our talents and creating something neither of us could have done in quite the same way alone. At first, it was about enjoying the music and expressing ourselves. But as we continued developing our sound and ideas, the possibility of taking it beyond college became real. We were two women from Detroit with a dream.

Parlé Mag: What were your creative responsibilities within Bo$$, and how did you contribute to building the group’s sound and vision?
Irene “Dee” Moore: One thing I want people to understand is that Bo$$ began as a creative partnership. My role wasn’t just about standing behind turntables. I was involved in the music and the creative direction of what we were building. Lichelle brought her energy and lyrical presence, while I contributed from the musical and DJ side. Hip-hop isn’t just about the person holding the microphone. It’s also about the sound, the arrangement, the atmosphere, and the people helping bring the vision together. Before the record labels and public attention, we were creating something together because we believed in it.

Parlé Mag: What was the experience of leaving Detroit and pursuing a music career in New York and Los Angeles like?
Irene “Dee” Moore: Leaving Detroit to pursue a music career was a major decision. When you’re chasing a dream, you don’t always know where the road will lead. You’re stepping away from everything familiar and entering an industry where nothing is guaranteed. New York and Los Angeles represented opportunity, but they also represented competition and sacrifice. What kept the dream alive was believing that we had something worth sharing with the world. That journey taught me that talent alone isn’t enough. You need determination, courage, patience, and the willingness to keep moving even when doors aren’t opening quickly.

Advertisement

Parlé Mag: As women entering the male-dominated gangsta rap scene, what challenges did you face, and how did those experiences shape your perspective?
Irene “Dee” Moore: Hip-hop was heavily male-dominated, especially the gangsta rap scene. As women, we were entering a space where people already had expectations about what we should look like, how we should sound, and what roles we should play. We had to show that women could bring the same creativity, strength, intelligence, and authenticity to the music. Those experiences helped me understand the importance of knowing my worth and not allowing someone else’s expectations to define my abilities. Women deserve recognition not only as performers but also as DJs, producers, creators, and decision-makers in hip-hop.

Parlé Mag: What did signing with Def Jam West mean for you and the vision you and Lichelle had been building?
Irene “Dee” Moore: The Def Jam West signing represented something much bigger than just a record deal. It was an opportunity for the music and the vision we had been working toward to reach a much larger audience. When you’re in the middle of pursuing your dream, you’re not necessarily thinking about making history. You’re thinking about the next step and how to make the most of the opportunity. Looking back, I appreciate the significance of being connected to that chapter of hip-hop, especially when women had limited opportunities in gangsta rap. It’s important that the full story is told and everyone who contributed receives recognition.

Parlé Mag: Looking back at Born Gangstaz, what creative contributions and musical ideas do you feel are important for people to understand about your involvement in the album?
Irene “Dee” Moore: When I think about Born Gangstaz, I think about the creative foundation that helped bring that project to life. People often focus on the person they see in front of the camera or hear on the microphone. But making music involves much more than that. There are creative decisions, musical ideas, arrangements, and contributions that help shape the finished product. I want people to understand that my involvement in Bo$$ was meaningful and that my role deserves to be part of the historical conversation. It’s about preserving the truth, honoring the work, and making sure future generations understand that women contributed to hip-hop in many different ways.

Advertisement

Parlé Mag: How important were album sequencing, atmosphere, and storytelling in shaping the overall listening experience of Born Gangstaz?
Irene “Dee” Moore: When you’re creating an album, it’s not just about putting songs together. It’s about creating an experience for the listener. The music, the energy, the transitions, and the storytelling all contribute to the identity of the project. My involvement in Bo$$ was about more than being a DJ. I brought my musical perspective, creativity, and understanding of hip-hop to the partnership. The person behind the turntables can be just as important to the creative process as the person behind the microphone. The sound of an album doesn’t happen by accident. I want people to recognize my contributions and include them in the history of Hip-Hop.

Parlé Mag: Throughout your journey, you used names such as DJ Dee, Gangsta-D, and Dee Tha Mad Bitch. What did each name represent about your personality and artistic identity?
Irene “Dee” Moore: Each name reflected a different side of my personality and artistic growth. DJ Dee captured my love for music and my beginnings as an artist. Gangsta-D showcased my fearless creativity, while Dee Tha Mad Bitch expressed my confidence, independence, and determination to prove myself.

Behind every name stood Irene Moore, a woman with her own identity, creativity, and ambitions. Through this journey, I learned that I could contribute to something bigger without losing sight of who I am.

Advertisement

Parlé Mag: Looking back at the 1993 separation, what lessons did you take away from the experience, particularly about creative partnerships and protecting your contributions?
Irene “Dee” Moore: When you’re young, talented, and pursuing something as big as a music career, you don’t always understand everything that comes with the business. Creative partnerships can be complicated because you’re dealing with friendships, professional responsibilities, personal goals, and outside influences. Looking back, one of the biggest lessons is the importance of understanding your value and protecting your creative identity. Artists, especially women, should understand their rights and document every contribution they make. I don’t want that chapter defined only by how things ended. I want people to recognize what we accomplished and what we helped create.

Parlé Mag: After stepping away from Bo$$, how did you begin establishing your identity and pursuing your ambitions beyond the group?
Irene “Dee” Moore: After stepping away from Bo$$, I had the opportunity to think about who I was beyond the group. I wanted my identity to reflect all of my abilities, not just one particular role in music. There is so much more to being an artist than what the public sees. There’s creativity, business, personal growth, and the freedom to develop your own vision. I wanted to establish my identity as Irene Moore, not just remain known for my connection to Bo$$. My story didn’t begin or end with that partnership. It was an important part of my journey, but not the entirety of who I was or what I could become.

Parlé Mag: When you think about Lichelle Laws, what stands out most about the journey you shared, and how do you hope people will remember her?
Irene “Dee” Moore: When I think about Lichelle, I remember a chapter of my life that began long before record deals, headlines, and fame. We were two young women from Detroit who shared a love for music and dared to pursue something bigger. No matter where life took us, that beginning will always remain part of our story.

Advertisement

I hope the next generation remembers Lichelle as a woman who challenged expectations and helped shape Hip-Hop. Her passing reminds us to celebrate people’s lives, preserve their stories, and honor their contributions. Both her story and mine deserve an honest, dignified, and respectful place in Hip-Hop history.

Parlé Mag: As you reflect on your journey, what do you hope your legacy will represent, and what can people expect from you moving forward?
Irene “Dee” Moore: When I think about my legacy, I look beyond records, performances, and my association with a famous name. I reflect on the journey, the sacrifices, and the courage it took to pursue my dream. Beyond my role behind the turntables, I want people to recognize Irene “Dee” Moore as a creative individual with her own talents, ideas, and vision. Women have always helped shape Hip-Hop, even when the industry overlooked their contributions. I don’t need to diminish anyone else’s legacy to establish my own. My legacy is about what I’ve contributed, learned, and can still give to the world.
